Oct 22 : Cable production capacity is emerging as a bottleneck for AI-driven data centre construction, Nexans' finance chief said, as demand rises faster than the industry's ability to expand manufacturing capacity. Global cable capacity is tight and building a new cross-linked polyethylene (XLPE) cable production line, known in the industry as a CV line, takes around three years, limiting how quickly suppliers can respond to demand, Nexans CFO Vincent Piquet told Reuters. "Things can't move quickly and the people building these data centres are in a great hurry," Piquet said. Data centres require large amounts of low- and medium-voltage cable to connect power infrastructure, with larger facilities consuming proportionately more medium-voltage cable.

The strain on power infrastructure is already delaying some projects. In September, Oracle issued a force majeure notice to a Blue Owl unit developing a large data centre in New Mexico, citing potential difficulties securing sufficient power for the site. Piquet said grid constraints, while slowing some projects, were also supporting demand for Nexans' products and allowing the company to be more selective when allocating capacity. French distribution network operator Enedis has moved from annual procurement agreements to contracts lasting six or seven years in order to secure cable supply, he said. While Europe generally faces fewer grid-connection challenges than the United States and benefits from stronger electricity networks in some northern countries, Piquet said lengthy regulatory processes were delaying certain projects. He said he did not expect demand linked to artificial intelligence to slow, although Europe's data-centre expansion was likely to be less pronounced than in the United States because private investment capacity was smaller and public funding played a larger role.

Source: Reuters

BRUSSELS, Oct 22 : Digital advertisers and publishers lobbied on Thursday for EU and UK regulators to suspend Meta Platforms' new commercial terms due to come into effect on October 30, alleging that these would give Meta an unlimited right to use their content for its AI services. Advocacy group the Movement for an Open Web, whose members include digital advertisers and publishers, said it had complained to the European Commission and the UK's Competition and Markets Authority and requested interim measures. Publishers worldwide are stepping up their fight with AI companies that use their content without permission to train large language models, underscoring the clash between copyright owners and those citing fair use arguments. "Meta's new terms are clearly anti-competitive. Many businesses effectively have no choice but to use Meta's services and these conditions would force them to sign away the rights to their digital content with no means of opting out," Tim Cowen, co-founder of the Movement for an Open Web, said.

"The terms would give Meta a free hand to scrape content from nearly every website in the world, potentially using that data to power AI-powered services that would then compete with those businesses," he said. Meta said it disagreed with the complaint. "The crawling terms we consolidated only applied to our ads and business products, and we've clarified that in the terms themselves. It does not change how Meta uses web crawlers," a Meta spokesperson said. "As always, content owners can use robots.txt to signal their preferences. This is not about scraping news sites, and these updates don't give us new rights that supersede those preferences." The CMA said it met with Meta on Wednesday to get more details on its new business terms. "This is an important issue and we recognise the concerns that have been raised by businesses in the UK. We are engaged in urgent discussions with Meta as we consider our next steps," a CMA spokesperson said. The European Commission did not immediately respond to emailed requests for comment. Companies requesting interim measures have to show that they will suffer serious and irreparable damage from the alleged anti-competitive practices. The criticism by the Movement for an Open Web followed similar complaints aired by the European Publishers Council (EPC) last week and Germany's Digital Publishers and Newspaper Publishers Association (BDZV) and the Association of the Free Press (MVFP) earlier this week.

Source: Reuters

Oct 22 : Nippon Steel will invest about $3 billion in the U.S. Steel-operated Mon Valley works in Pennsylvania to upgrade the plant's hot rolling facility, the Nikkei newspaper reported on Thursday. The move is part of the Japanese steelmaker's pledge to invest $11 billion in U.S. Steel by 2028, following its acquisition of the company in 2025. Nippon Steel did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment outside regular business hours. Mon Valley's hot rolling equipment, which heats slabs of iron from blast furnaces and rolls them into thinner steel, has been in operation for about 90 years, Nikkei added. The new equipment is set to enter operation in the second half of 2029, which would enable production of higher-quality steel, the report said. Nippon Steel raised its fiscal 2026 earnings forecast in August, lifted by stronger U.S. Steel earnings and a firm steel market.

Source: Reuters

Oct 22 : Anyone who has watched a manta ray glide over a reef knows how unhurried these marine animals can look. Yet researchers working off Costa Rica found their movements are varied, with juveniles staying nearby and close to shore while adults venture hundreds of kilometres. Manta rays are among the ocean's largest fish, with wing-like fins that can span up to about 8 meters (26 feet) and the largest brain of any fish. Researchers tracked endangered oceanic manta rays between 2018 and 2025, fitting 59 of them with acoustic transmitters and tracking 12 with satellite tags, along with photo identification.  "By combining different technologies ... we were able to piece together a highly detailed map of their movements and their use of coastal cleaning stations," said Jeffry Madrigal-Mesén, director of the research group Mantas Costa Rica and lead author of the study published in the journal Frontiers in Fish Science.

A coastal cleaning station is a rocky reef site where small fish remove parasites from the skin of the manta rays in an example of symbiotic behaviour. Researchers found that smaller, immature mantas stayed within Costa Rica's coastal waters, called its exclusive economic zone. Larger, mature animals undertook long-distance journeys, some reaching as far as the waters off Guatemala. "This makes us believe that smaller mantas do not risk these long migrations, likely due to the threat of large predators like orcas and tiger sharks," Madrigal-Mesén said. The smaller animals in the study measured around 3 to 3.5 meters across (10 to 11.5 feet), compared with around 4 to 4.5 meters (13 to 15 feet) for those making the longer journeys. DANGER FROM PREDATORS A juvenile, at around 3 meters across, would still appear enormous to most swimmers. Yet that size may not be enough protection. Madrigal-Mesén said that "their massive size is one of their main defence mechanisms. It is quite common to see animals missing portions of their bodies, and in many cases, the shape of the wounds strongly suggests they are bites from other large marine predators." What prompts mantas to eventually join the migratory population remains unclear, although researchers suspect that reaching feeding and breeding grounds in highly productive waters across Central America may play a role. The manta rays also repeatedly return to the same coastal cleaning stations. Observations of feeding, courtship and recent mating suggest these sites may also function as social hubs. Scientists do not yet know how mantas navigate back to particular sites. "Based on the bathymetry of the different sites we monitor, there must be a relationship with the rock formations. We humans have favourite places we like to go to," Madrigal-Mesén said. "Why couldn't mantas have a preference for one cleaning station over another?" The findings also suggest the mantas may not roam as far as once thought. Researchers initially suspected that animals seen in Costa Rica might migrate from populations in Ecuador or Mexico. The tracking data instead raises the possibility that Central America has its own distinct population, something the team is now investigating through genetic work. Mantas are particularly vulnerable because, like other rays and sharks, they reproduce slowly and take years to reach sexual maturity. Madrigal-Mesén said that once the animals left Cocos Island, a volcanic island in the Pacific Ocean, and most monitored coastal sites, they entered waters with no protection, exposing them to threats including fishing and vessel traffic. "Studies like this help us recognise that these coastal havens only protect them for a specific time of the year. ... This is why it is so critical to protect the marine corridors these migratory species travel through." Coastal mantas also showed strong site fidelity, with very few moving between monitoring sites even when they were only tens of kilometres apart.  One male became a particularly striking example. Nicknamed "Mickey Mouse" for its distinctive spot pattern, the ray was repeatedly photographed at Cabo Blanco and tracked using both satellite and acoustic tags, showing a strong attachment to the site.  But researchers have not seen this ray in Costa Rica for more than a year.  "We have a lot of affection for him," Madrigal-Mesén added. "We hope he comes back soon."

Source: Reuters

FAST

NEW YORK, Oct 22 : The yen was on track for its strongest daily gain in almost a month on Thursday, as investors sought safety amid fragile equity markets, elevated crude prices from the drawn-out war in the Middle East, and doubts over future returns from artificial intelligence. The US dollar, meanwhile, rose against the euro. Worries about social unrest in France and a worsening fiscal outlook for the country outweighed concerns about the AI trade, which pushed US stocks lower. "AI is making people nervous, as is oil ... and as is France, and obviously we have a slight degree of risk aversion in the market," said Chris Scicluna, head of economic research at Daiwa Capital Markets. Brent crude climbed to its highest level since May after further Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia raised fears of an escalation in the Middle East conflict and more disruption to oil supplies from the key exporting region.

The Japanese yen strengthened 0.51 per cent to 157.33 per dollar.  The Swiss franc, another traditional safe haven, was little changed at 0.824 per dollar. The dollar index, which measures the greenback against a basket of currencies including the yen and the euro, rose 0.14 per cent to 101.82, with the euro down 0.3 per cent at $1.1198. The dollar has become increasingly tied to capital flows and to growth and inflation expectations linked to the AI trade. It fell last week as fears over the AI outlook grew. On Thursday, however, concerns about France outweighed those fears. “You have these competing stories and weak points between US AI-related credits and then France sovereign credit, and we've seen this push and pull in the last couple of days where at times one is more of a concern than the other,” said Erik Nelson, global head of FX strategy at Wells Fargo. “As long as France is more of a concern than US AI credits, then you're going to see the euro underperform.” French President Emmanuel Macron vowed on Wednesday to prevent a repeat of last weekend's violence at protests planned in the coming days, and dismissed as "stupid" and "unacceptable" comments from some foreign leaders about the unrest. Concerns about France's ability to manage its huge debt burden have hurt French government bonds and raised worries about other heavily indebted euro zone countries. The spread between France and Germany's 10-year note yields reached 177.7 basis points on Thursday, the widest gap since 2011. Sterling weakened 0.18 per cent to $1.337. The Australian dollar fell 0.21 per cent to $0.7012. In cryptocurrencies, bitcoin fell 3.20 per cent to $81,929.  (Additional reporting by Amanda Cooper and Tom Westbrook; Editing by Xevi Fontdegloria)

Source: Reuters

Oct 22 : A once-robust fall calendar for technology IPOs is down to just Anthropic. The AI lab is pressing ahead to hold its initial public offering as planned in the middle of next month after making its  prospectus public as early as late October, people familiar with the matter said, cautioning the plan and the dates are subject to change.  Anthropic's planned IPO will test whether its position at the center of the booming AI business, which the company is believed to deem worthy of a potential $1.5 trillion valuation, can overcome a market environment that might typically prompt bankers and deal lawyers to counsel delay. Anthropic is expected to begin marketing its shares to prospective investors during the week of November 9, one of the people said. Other companies in the artificial intelligence infrastructure and data center sectors have delayed their listings, facing a rise in interest rates that has helped fuel a punishing selloff in shares and bonds of AI operators such as CoreWeave and broader questions about the sustainability of AI spending.

The contrast underscores Anthropic's appeal to investors even as concerns about competition from open-source models and AI safety weigh on the sector.  Many  large investors remain bullish on Anthropic’s prospects despite the fall turbulence, viewing the firm as one of the few opportunities to gain exposure to a technology sector that long-term investors cannot afford to ignore. Other issuers are reluctant to compete with Anthropic for institutional investors' attention and capital, two of the people said. Anthropic didn't immediately respond to a request for comment. VALUATIONS COMING UNDER PRESSURE The AI sector pullback follows a string of IPO delays and withdrawals since September, as market volatility and rising interest rates have made it harder for companies to secure attractive valuations. Switch, a data center operator, and Nscale, an AI infrastructure provider, have pushed their IPO plans back to later this year, people familiar with the matter said, while stressing that plans remain fluid and subject to change. Nscale’s delay was partly driven by the need to address comments from SEC staff, one other person said. SoftBank-backed SB Energy has also postponed its listing, Reuters previously reported. Switch, NScale and SB Energy didn't immediately respond to requests for comment. South Korean AI chip startup Elice was among the latest to shelve its listing plans overnight. Blackstone-backed AirTrunk REIT and Nvidia-backed Firmus have also pulled or paused their offerings, Reuters has reported. Oura's recent IPO has added to the caution among prospective issuers. The offering attracted little participation from long-only investors, a person familiar with the matter said, raising concerns about the depth of demand from institutional investors that typically provide a stable base of shareholders for newly listed companies. SCRUTINY ON MULTIPLE FRONTS The retreat from AI infrastructure listings reflects growing scrutiny of the enormous capital required to build data centers and whether future demand will justify the investment. Recent developments involving CoreWeave have added to concerns about a potential slowdown in AI spending, although some market participants do not expect such a downturn to materialize. Nscale publicly filed its IPO registration statement in September, while Switch submitted its filing confidentially, Reuters reported previously. A confidential filing allows a company to work with regulators on its registration statement before disclosing financial and business details to the public. Companies typically publish the filing ahead of investor roadshows, when they begin marketing shares to prospective investors.

As a condition of funding, the US government will receive minority, non-controlling and non-voting equity stakes, the department said. In recent months, it has awarded 19 R&D grants to semiconductor firms from a $10 billion fund approved by Congress in 2022. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick said in a statement the awards will "accelerate American semiconductor innovation to enhance our domestic energy and power resources." Oct 22 : Indian digital trust services provider eMudhra on Thursday said it would voluntarily withdraw from the global SSL/TLS certificate business, following an incident in which its digital certificates were found to have vulnerabilities. The disclosure of the vulnerabilities led to internet browser majors such as Google, Mozilla, Apple and Microsoft to block digital certificates issued by eMudhra, and sparked larger concerns among cybersecurity professionals around internet security and privacy. SSL and TLS are protocols used to secure data sent between web browsers and servers, ensuring that private information cannot be intercepted by bad actors. eMudhra issues these certificates to digital businesses and government agencies, including for some online public services such as India's income tax portal. An independent cybersecurity researcher found over the weekend that several key certificates issued by eMudhra, used to secure websites, software, and online communications, were weak and vulnerable to attack.

"Too much money in the digital asset ecosystem is sitting idle, leaving massive potential earnings on the table for millions of people," SoFi CEO Anthony Noto told Reuters. The product moves SoFi into a space historically dominated by non-bank crypto firms. In recent years, funds earmarked for crypto trading were often parked in interest-bearing stablecoins, giving investors a way to earn yield while keeping money ready to deploy. That model has come under pressure after the GENIUS Act, signed last year, barred stablecoin issuers from paying interest, creating an opening for banks to offer regulated, interest-bearing alternatives through products such as tokenized deposits. SoFi Earn will also let users buy crypto directly or transfer funds to another platform. "The primary opportunity is with people who already participate in crypto and want that money to keep working and ready to move," Noto said. Traditional financial institutions are developing products to tap the crypto market, arguing that bank-issued alternatives offer greater regulatory oversight than stablecoins issued by non-bank entities. In September, a group of 21 financial institutions including Goldman Sachs, Bank of America, Citi and Deutsche Bank, said they planned to create a company this year to issue a dollar-pegged cryptocurrency in the first half of 2027. "Over the next year or so, you're going to see an inflection point. It is a big effort to move traditional finance on chain, but I think the economic drivers are just so powerful that it's inevitable," said Sam MacPherson, CEO at digital asset finance firm Spark.

Oct 22 : Tesla's shares fell 2 per cent on Thursday after the EV maker cut its capital spending forecast, raising concerns among investors counting on heavy investment for Elon Musk's AI and robotics vision. The company on Wednesday lowered its 2026 capital spending forecast to about $20 billion from more than $25 billion after spending far less than expected on AI and robotics in the third quarter, which led to a surprise positive free cash flow. The strong position may prove valuable as CEO Musk explores combining Tesla with the far more capital-intensive SpaceX. Oct 22 : Artificial intelligence could boost global growth, but poorer countries, smaller companies and younger workers risk missing out unless access to power, digital infrastructure and skills improves, according to officials from the IMF and OECD. The warning comes as massive investment in chips and AI infrastructure has helped support global growth and drive stock markets to record highs, while raising concerns about whether companies can generate sufficient returns on large spending commitments as borrowing costs rise. "For many developing economies, the critical question is whether they can adopt and diffuse AI," Era Dabla-Norris, deputy director of the International Monetary Fund's Fiscal Affairs Department, told the Reuters Global Markets Forum. Effective AI adoption could add up to 0.5 per cent to annual global growth over the medium term, the IMF estimates.

"But the aggregate productivity evidence, so far, is much less," Dabla-Norris said. The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development estimates AI could add 0.4 per cent to 1.2 per cent to annual productivity growth across its member countries. But its chief economist, Stefano Scarpetta, said that workplace use trails consumer use, with only limited adoption in core business functions. "There is a large gap between exposure and actual use," Scarpetta said. The IMF estimates that about 40 per cent of jobs worldwide could be exposed to AI, as reports of mass layoffs gather pace. Barclays said it was cutting around 5,000 jobs this year as it uses technology including AI to reduce costs and improve returns. EBay is reported to be laying off 9 per cent of its workforce, while Qualcomm is expected to cut jobs globally in a "performance-focused reduction". Dabla-Norris said younger and entry-level workers could be particularly vulnerable if AI takes over tasks through which employees traditionally gain experience. Oct 22 : Publishing group Axel Springer would welcome any European initiative to separate TikTok from its Chinese owners along the lines of President Donald Trump's deal to split the US social media app from its parent, a spokesperson for the German company said on Thursday. TikTok's Chinese owner, ByteDance, finalised a deal in January to transfer control of TikTok's US operations to an American-owned joint venture. The aim was to avert a ban in the US on the short-video app to allay security concerns raised by US politicians regarding the Chinese ownership of the app, which is popular with over 200 million Americans. The comment from Axel Springer, owner of Politico, Telegraph Media Group and Business Insider, came in response to a Financial Times report. According to the report, Springer's CEO and co-owner Mathias Doepfner - who has repeatedly criticised TikTok - pitched an idea during a lunch in January with the US Ambassador to France, Charles Kushner, in which his company could be part of a deal to buy TikTok's European operations. "As is clear from his public statements, Mathias Doepfner has always advocated for a European solution for TikTok along the lines of the American model," the spokesperson told Reuters. "Had such a solution materialized, Axel Springer would have welcomed the opportunity to be part of it as a major European media player."

Oct 22 : Meta Platforms has a strong basis for arguing that the $25 billion penalty New Mexico secured this week in a case stemming from allegations the firm mishandled user data should be reduced on appeal, legal experts said.  The judgment was one of the largest state verdicts against a company in US history. It came after a jury found Meta misled consumers about who had access to their data in the wake of revelations that Cambridge Analytica, a political consulting firm involved in President Donald Trump's 2016 presidential campaign, had harvested personal data from millions of Facebook users.  New Mexico said state law allowed for a penalty of up to $5,000 for each time someone in the state may have seen an allegedly misleading statement from Meta. Experts said the company would likely argue that Judge Francis Mathew should only have considered people who actually saw the statements.   "The most vulnerable basis on appeal is going to be the question about whether a violation is going to count, even in the absence of any proof that a particular person saw one of these misrepresentations or relied on them to their detriment," said Peter Ormerod, a law professor at Villanova University.

C.J. Mahoney, Meta's chief legal officer, said the company is confident it will win on appeal. The company is expected to appeal the underlying jury verdict and the penalty. Meta has previously said that it does not sell user data and that New Mexico did not prove any consumer had actually been misled and that a penalty in the billions of dollars would risk violating its constitutional rights to due process and protection from excessive fines.  New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez said on Wednesday he expected Meta to appeal the judgment and the state stood ready to defend its legal position. He did not immediately respond to a request for further comment. JURY FOUND 43 MILLION VIOLATIONS New Mexico's attorney general sued Meta in 2021, alleging that the company lied to Facebook users about who had access to their data, how the company handled hate speech and misinformation posted on the platform, and other internal policies.  Jurors on September 25 found that 26 of 29 statements made by the company and its leadership on those issues were misleading. Multiplying those statements by their potential audience within New Mexico, the jury said the company had committed more than 43 million violations of the state’s consumer protection laws. The state had 1.4 million active Facebook users and a population of 2.1 million as of 2020.  Mathew said in his ruling on Wednesday that a penalty of more than $219 billion would be justified under state law, which allows a $5,000 penalty for each violation, but he reduced the amount. The state had urged Mathew to award the state between $35 billion and $40 billion, while Meta said penalties of no more than $3.45 billion were warranted.  Ormerod said that even if the company's appeals in state courts fail, Meta could argue to the US Supreme Court that the penalty violated its rights under the US Constitution to due process and against excessive fines.  The size of the penalty on its own does not mean it will be overturned, given the New Mexico law allowing for penalties for each willful violation, said Daryl Lim, a professor at Penn State Dickinson Law.  But it seems implausible that Meta was really responsible for so much financial harm, a sign the penalty may be unjust, said Eric Goldman, a professor at Santa Clara University School of Law. "It felt like there was a lot of duplicative counting in the calculations," Goldman said. "How many times can a single person be duped by the same entity?"

Source: Reuters
